\">\u003cfigcaption>Figure · page 1\u003c/figcaption>\u003c/figure>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">UPPER GASTROINTESTINAL\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">BLEEDING (UGIB)\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">LET’S FIRST KNOW THE COMPLICATION\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">ACUTE COMPLICATIONS OF UPPER GASTROINTESTINAL BLEEDING\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Acute complications occur during or shortly after the bleeding episode and are mainly related\u003cbr>to hemorrhage, hypoperfusion, and systemic instability.\u003c/p>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Acute Complication\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Explanation\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Hypovolemic shock\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Massive blood loss causes reduced circulating\u003cbr>volume leading to hypotension, tachycardia, poor\u003cbr>organ perfusion, and shock\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Acute blood loss anemia\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Rapid loss of red blood cells causes reduced oxygen\u003cbr>delivery resulting in weakness, dizziness, syncope,\u003cbr>and tissue hypoxia\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Hemodynamic instability\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Persistent bleeding may cause severe hypotension\u003cbr>and cardiovascular collapse\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 2\u003c/div>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Myocardial\u003cbr>ischemia/infarction\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Reduced oxygen delivery may precipitate cardiac\u003cbr>ischemia especially in elderly or patients with\u003cbr>coronary artery disease\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Acute kidney injury (AKI)\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Renal hypoperfusion from shock leads to prerenal\u003cbr>AKI or acute tubular injury\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Aspiration pneumonia\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Hematemesis may be aspirated into lungs causing\u003cbr>respiratory compromise and infection\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Respiratory failure\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Severe anemia, aspiration, or shock may impair\u003cbr>oxygenation\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Rebleeding\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Early recurrent hemorrhage may occur especially in\u003cbr>peptic ulcer disease or variceal bleeding\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Coagulopathy\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Massive bleeding, liver disease, or transfusion-\u003cbr>related dilution may impair coagulation\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Lactic acidosis\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Tissue hypoperfusion during shock leads to\u003cbr>anaerobic metabolism and lactate accumulation\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Multiorgan dysfunction\u003cbr>syndrome (MODS)\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Severe prolonged shock may result in failure of\u003cbr>kidneys, liver, lungs, and cardiovascular system\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Death\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Severe uncontrolled hemorrhage may rapidly become\u003cbr>fatal\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">CHRONIC / LONG-TERM COMPLICATIONS OF UPPER GASTROINTESTINAL BLEEDING\u003c/h3>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Chronic Complication\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Explanation\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Chronic iron deficiency\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Recurrent occult or overt bleeding causes gradual\u003cbr>depletion of iron stores\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>anemia\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Recurrent UGIB\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Recurrent UGIB\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Persistent ulcers, varices, malignancy, or NSAID use may\u003cbr>lead to repeated bleeding episodes\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Hepatic\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>In variceal bleeding, cirrhotic patients may develop\u003cbr>worsening liver failure\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>decompensation\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Hepatic encephalopathy\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Hepatic encephalopathy\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>GI blood increases intestinal nitrogen load leading to\u003cbr>ammonia accumulation in cirrhosis\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Portal hypertensive\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Ascites, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, and hepatorenal\u003cbr>syndrome may worsen after variceal hemorrhage\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>complications\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Esophageal strictures\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Esophageal strictures\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Recurrent inflammation or endoscopic therapy may rarely\u003cbr>cause fibrosis and narrowing\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Malnutrition\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Chronic illness, liver disease, or recurrent bleeding\u003cbr>contributes to nutritional deficiency\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Transfusion-related\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Repeated transfusions may cause iron overload,\u003cbr>alloimmunization, or transfusion reactions\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>complications\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Psychological morbidity\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Psychological morbidity\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Recurrent severe bleeding may cause anxiety, depression,\u003cbr>or reduced quality of life\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Increased long-term\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Especially in elderly patients, malignancy, or advanced\u003cbr>cirrhosis\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>mortality\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003c/section>\u003csection -ENDOSCOPY\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. Initial Stabilization and Resuscitation\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Initial stabilization is the most critical step in the management of upper gastrointestinal\u003cbr>bleeding because mortality in UGIB is commonly caused by hemorrhagic shock, aspiration,\u003cbr>multiorgan failure, or delayed resuscitation rather than the lesion itself. According to\u003cbr>Davidson’s Principles and Practice of Medicine, Harrison’s Internal Medicine, and\u003cbr>international gastroenterology guidelines, the first priority is stabilization of airway,\u003cbr>breathing, and circulation before definitive diagnostic or therapeutic procedures such as\u003cbr>endoscopy are performed.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The main objectives during the resuscitation phase are:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">❖ restoration of circulating blood volume,\u003cbr>❖ maintenance of tissue perfusion,\u003cbr>❖ prevention of shock,\u003cbr>❖ stabilization before endoscopy,\u003cbr>❖ and prevention of early complications such as aspiration and acute kidney injury.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Assessment of Hemodynamic Status\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 4\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The first step is rapid assessment of hemodynamic stability because the severity of blood loss\u003cbr>determines urgency of intervention.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Clinical signs suggesting significant hemorrhage include:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">1. tachycardia,\u003cbr>2. hypotension,\u003cbr>3. narrow pulse pressure,\u003cbr>4. cold clammy extremities,\u003cbr>5. delayed capillary refill,\u003cbr>6. dizziness or syncope,\u003cbr>7. altered mental status,\u003cbr>8. and reduced urine output.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Patients with severe ongoing bleeding may rapidly progress to:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">1. hemorrhagic shock,\u003cbr>2. lactic acidosis,\u003cbr>3. acute kidney injury,\u003cbr>4. myocardial ischemia,\u003cbr>5. and multiorgan dysfunction.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">According to emergency medicine principles, early recognition of circulatory compromise is\u003cbr>essential because tissue hypoperfusion may occur before laboratory hemoglobin levels fall\u003cbr>significantly.\u003c/p>\u003cfigure class=\"note-figure\">\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" alt=\"Illustration associated with page 4\" src=\"data:image/webp;base64,\">\u003cfigcaption>Figure · page 4\u003c/figcaption>\u003c/figure>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Airway and Breathing\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 5\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Airway assessment is performed immediately because massive hematemesis can compromise\u003cbr>airway patency and lead to aspiration.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Patients at high risk of airway compromise include:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">1. massive active hematemesis,\u003cbr>2. hepatic encephalopathy,\u003cbr>3. altered consciousness,\u003cbr>4. severe agitation,\u003cbr>5. respiratory distress,\u003cbr>6. or inability to protect the airway.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">In these patients, endotracheal intubation may be required before endoscopy.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Breathing assessment includes:\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. respiratory rate,   2. oxygen saturation,   3. work of breathing,   4. and evidence of aspiration.\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Supplemental oxygen is administered if hypoxia is present. Continuous pulse oximetry\u003cbr>monitoring is important because oxygen delivery may be impaired both by hypovolemia and\u003cbr>acute blood loss anemia.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Intravenous Access and Fluid Resuscitation\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">According to current UGIB protocols, two large-bore intravenous cannulas (16G or 18G)\u003cbr>should be inserted immediately because rapid fluid and blood administration may become\u003cbr>necessary.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Initial fluid therapy usually begins with isotonic crystalloids such as:\u003c/p>\u003cfigure class=\"note-figure\">\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" alt=\"Illustration associated with page 5\" src=\"data:image/webp;base64,\">\u003cfigcaption>Figure · page 5\u003c/figcaption>\u003c/figure>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. Ringer’s lactate,   2. or normal saline.\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Crystalloids temporarily restore:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  intravascular volume,   •  preload,   •  cardiac output,   •  and tissue perfusion.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">If bleeding is ongoing and blood products are not immediately available, colloids may\u003cbr>occasionally be considered, although crystalloids remain first-line in most modern protocols.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The patient should remain:\u003c/p>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Nil by mouth (NPO) because urgent endoscopy, intubation, or surgery may become\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>necessary\u003c/td>\u003ctd>.\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 6\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Continuous monitoring should include:\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. blood pressure,\u003cbr>2. pulse rate,\u003cbr>3. oxygen saturation,\u003cbr>4. respiratory rate,\u003cbr>5. mental status,\u003cbr>6. and urine output.\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Urine output is a major bedside indicator of renal perfusion and adequacy of resuscitation.\u003cbr>The target urine output is generally:&gt;0.5 mL/kg/hour\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Initial Blood Investigations\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Blood should be drawn immediately during IV access placement.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Important investigations include:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">1. Full blood count,\u003cbr>2. Blood grouping and crossmatch,\u003cbr>3. Urea, creatinine, and electrolytes,\u003cbr>4. Liver function tests,\u003cbr>5. PT/INR and coagulation profile,\u003cbr>6. Platelet count,\u003cbr>7. Random blood glucose,\u003cbr>8. HIV testing where appropriate,\u003cbr>9. Hepatitis screening in suspected chronic liver disease.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">One important classical finding in upper GI bleeding is a disproportionately elevated blood\u003cbr>urea nitrogen (BUN). This occurs because digested blood proteins are absorbed from the\u003cbr>intestine and metabolized into urea by the liver.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>BUN is very high compared with creatinine, often with a BUN: Creatinine ratio &gt;20:1\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>and the rise is greater than what would be expected from kidney dysfunction alone.\u003c/p>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Condition\u003c/td>\u003ctd>BUN\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Creatinine\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Ratio\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Upper GI bleed\u003c/td>\u003ctd>40 mg/dL\u003c/td>\u003ctd>1.0 mg/dL\u003c/td>\u003ctd>40:1\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Intrinsic renal failure\u003c/td>\u003ctd>40 mg/dL\u003c/td>\u003ctd>4.0 mg/dL\u003c/td>\u003ctd>10:1\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">In UGIB, creatinine may remain near normal initially, but BUN rises markedly because of  absorbed digested blood.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Blood Transfusion Strategy\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Blood transfusion is one of the most important and carefully controlled components of UGIB\u003cbr>resuscitation.Modern management follows a: Restrictive transfusion strategy\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">According to major trials and hepatology guidelines:\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 7\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>Packed red blood cells are generally transfused when hemoglobin falls below\u003cbr>approximately 7 g/dL in most patients,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>While higher-risk patients may require transfusion at hemoglobin levels below\u003cbr>approximately 9 g/dL.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">High-risk patients include:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>elderly patients,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>patients with cardiovascular disease,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>ischemic heart disease,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>severe hypoxia,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>persistent shock,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>or ongoing massive hemorrhage.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The usual target hemoglobin is:7–9 g/Dl rather than complete normalization.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The reason excessive transfusion is avoided is because overtransfusion increases:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  intravascular volume,   •  portal venous pressure,   •  and risk of recurrent hemorrhage.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">This is especially dangerous in: Variceal bleeding because increased portal pressure may\u003cbr>dislodge newly formed clots and precipitate recurrent variceal rupture.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">According to Harrison’s Internal Medicine and portal hypertension guidelines, liberal\u003cbr>transfusion strategies in cirrhotic patients are associated with increased rebleeding and\u003cbr>mortality due to worsening portal hypertension.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">One unit of packed red blood cells usually raises hemoglobin by approximately:1 g/dL\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">In emergency situations with profound instability:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  type-specific blood,   •  or O-negative blood\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">may be required before full crossmatching is completed.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">In massive hemorrhage or severe coagulopathy, additional blood products may include:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Fresh frozen plasma (FFP),   •  Platelets,   •  Cryoprecipitate in selected cases.   •\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Hemodynamic Goals During Resuscitation\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The purpose of resuscitation is restoration of organ perfusion while avoiding overtransfusion.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Common targets include:\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 8\u003c/div>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Parameter\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Target\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Mean arterial pressure\u003c/td>\u003ctd>&gt;65 mmHg\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Urine output\u003c/td>\u003ctd>&gt;0.5 mL/kg/hr\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Oxygen saturation\u003c/td>\u003ctd>&gt;94%\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Heart rate\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Improving\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Mental status\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Improving\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Lactate\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Falling\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Persistent hypotension despite fluids and blood may indicate:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  ongoing active hemorrhage,  •  delayed control of bleeding,\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  sepsis,  •  adrenal insufficiency,  •  or multiorgan failure.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Important Clinical Pearls\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>Hemoglobin may initially appear normal in acute massive hemorrhage before plasma\u003cbr>equilibration occurs.\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Tachycardia is often an early sign of significant blood loss.\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Over transfusion is particularly dangerous in portal hypertensive bleeding because it\u003cbr>increases portal pressure and risk of rebleeding.\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Airway protection is essential before endoscopy in unstable patients.\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Stabilization should always occur before definitive diagnostic procedures.\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>HCT &lt;21–25% usually indicates severe anemia requiring urgent\u003cbr>evaluation/transfusion depending on clinical state.\u003c/p>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>• HCT &lt;21–25% usually indicates severe anemia requiring urgent\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>evaluation/transfusion depending on clinical state.\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>2. HAEMOSTASIS (STOPPING THE BLEEDING) IN UPPER\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>GASTROINTESTINAL BLEEDING\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">After initial stabilization and restoration of circulating volume, the next major objective in\u003cbr>upper gastrointestinal bleeding is:haemostasis\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Haemostasis refers to all interventions aimed at stopping active bleeding, stabilizing clot\u003cbr>formation, preventing early rebleeding, and reducing mortality. According to Harrison’s\u003cbr>Internal Medicine, Davidson’s Principles and Practice of Medicine, ACG guidelines, and\u003cbr>portal hypertension guidelines, haemostasis in UGIB involves a combination of:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">1. pharmacological therapy,\u003cbr>2. mechanical measures,\u003cbr>3. endoscopic intervention,\u003cbr>4. and sometimes radiological or surgical procedures.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The choice of hemostatic therapy depends on:\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 9\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">1. the source of bleeding,\u003cbr>2. hemodynamic stability,\u003cbr>3. presence of cirrhosis or portal hypertension,\u003cbr>4. and endoscopic findings.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The two major categories are:\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. variceal bleeding,   2. and non-variceal bleeding.\u003c/h3>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Pharmacological Haemostasis\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Medical therapy should begin immediately after stabilization and should not wait for\u003cbr>endoscopy if clinical suspicion is high.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Proton Pump Inhibitors (PPIs)\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">PPIs are mainly used in: Non-variceal bleeding especially:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">❖ peptic ulcer disease,   ❖ erosive gastritis,   ❖ and high-risk ulcer bleeding.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Commonly used PPIs include:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">❖ Pantoprazole,   ❖ Omeprazole,   ❖ Esomeprazole.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">According to international UGIB guidelines, high-dose intravenous PPI therapy is\u003cbr>recommended in suspected peptic ulcer bleeding before endoscopy because it helps stabilize\u003cbr>clots and reduces rebleeding risk.A common regimen is:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">✓ Pantoprazole 80 mg IV bolus,  followed by 8 mg/hour continuous infusion.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The mechanism of PPIs Proton Pump Inhibitors\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">This increases gastric pH above 6, which:\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. stabilizes blood clots,\u003cbr>2. improves platelet aggregation,\u003cbr>3. reduces fibrinolysis,\u003cbr>4. and promotes mucosal healing.\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The mechanism of PPIs Proton Pump Inhibitors are medications that suppress gastric acid\u003cbr>secretion by irreversibly inhibiting the hydrogen-potassium ATPase (H+/K+ ATPase) proton\u003cbr>pump located on gastric parietal cells, which is the final pathway responsible for acid\u003cbr>production in the stomach. By markedly increasing gastric pH, PPIs stabilize blood clots over\u003cbr>bleeding ulcers, reduce clot breakdown by acid and pepsin, promote mucosal healing, and\u003cbr>decrease the risk of recurrent hemorrhage\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 10\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Acidic gastric environments destabilize platelet plugs and interfere with coagulation;\u003cbr>therefore, acid suppression is extremely important in ulcer-related hemorrhage.According to\u003cbr>ACG and ESGE guidelines, pre-endoscopic PPI therapy may reduce high-risk endoscopic\u003cbr>stigmata and need for endoscopic therapy.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Somatostatin Analogues (Octreotide)\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Octreotide is primarily used in: Variceal bleeding especially in patients with:\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. cirrhosis,   2. portal hypertension,   3. esophageal varices,   4. or suspected portal hypertensive hemorrhage.\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">According to hepatology guidelines, vasoactive therapy should be started immediately once\u003cbr>variceal bleeding is suspected, even before endoscopy. The standard regimen is:\u003c/p>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>1. Octreotide 50 micrograms IV bolus, followed by 50 micrograms/hour infusion,\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>usually continued for 2–5 days.\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The mechanism of octreotide involves:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">1. splanchnic vasoconstriction,\u003cbr>2. reduced portal venous inflow,\u003cbr>3. reduced portal pressure,\u003cbr>4. and reduced variceal wall tension.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Somatostatin is a naturally occurring inhibitory peptide hormone produced mainly in\u003cbr>the hypothalamus, pancreas, and gastrointestinal tract that suppresses the release of\u003cbr>several hormones and gastrointestinal secretions, including growth hormone, insulin,\u003cbr>glucagon, and gastrin. It also reduces splanchnic blood flow through vasoconstriction,\u003cbr>thereby lowering portal venous pressure; because natural somatostatin has a very\u003cbr>short half-life, synthetic analogues such as Octreotide are commonly used clinically,\u003cbr>especially in acute variceal bleeding and portal hypertension.\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 11\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Octreotide acts by mimicking somatostatin and causing selective vasoconstriction of\u003cbr>the splanchnic circulation, which reduces portal venous inflow and lowers portal\u003cbr>hypertension. This decreases pressure and wall tension within esophageal varices,\u003cbr>helping control hemorrhage, promote hemostasis, and reduce the risk of early\u003cbr>rebleeding in acute variceal bleeding associated with cirrhosis and portal\u003cbr>hypertension.\u003c/p>\u003cfigure class=\"note-figure\">\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" alt=\"Illustration associated with page 11\" src=\"data:image/webp;base64,
